title: Sum Only Visible Cells Filtered
description: Learn how to sum only visible cells filtered data with SUBTOTAL codes 9 and 109, why a plain SUM keeps hidden rows, and the SUMPRODUCT criteria trick.
intro: Apply a filter and every plain SUM on the sheet keeps counting the rows you just hid. SUBTOTAL is the one built-in aggregate that follows the filter. This guide covers the exact formulas for summing visible rows, the difference between function codes 9 and 109, and how to add criteria on top of a filtered list.
prerequisites: Comfort with basic SUM and absolute references (the $ signs)
A table with an AutoFilter applied
Google Sheets users: no AGGREGATE available, use SUBTOTAL

sections.title: Why Plain SUM Counts Rows You Cannot See
sections.content: An AutoFilter hides rows visually, it does not remove them from the grid. SUM, SUMIF and SUMIFS read every cell in the range regardless of visibility, so a filtered table keeps reporting the grand total. That mismatch is the single most common reason a dashboard total disagrees with the rows on screen. The sample used throughout this guide has products in A2:A7 and amounts of 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 and 600 in C2:C7, for a full total of 2100.

example.explanation: With the table filtered to Product = Widget, rows 3, 5 and 7 are hidden. SUM still adds all six amounts and returns 2100, while only 100 + 300 + 500 is actually on screen.

tips: Never drop a plain SUM under a filtered list if the number is meant to follow the filter.
SUMIF and SUMIFS share the same blind spot — they have no idea which rows are hidden.

sections.title: SUBTOTAL with Code 9: The Standard Fix
sections.content: SUBTOTAL is filter-aware. Function code 9 means SUM, and rows hidden by an AutoFilter are excluded no matter which code you use — Google's own documentation states this rule for both Excel and Google Sheets. The formulas below use absolute references so the range survives dragging and copying.

steps.name: Turn on the filter
steps.text: Select the header row and enable filtering: Data > Filter in Excel, Data > Create a filter in Google Sheets.

steps.name: Point SUBTOTAL at the amount column
steps.text: Use code 9 for SUM and keep the range to the data rows only.

steps.name: Change the filter and watch it follow
steps.text: The result recalculates from the visible rows only. No refresh, no macro, no helper column.

example.explanation: Filtered to Widget, rows 2, 4 and 6 stay visible (100 + 300 + 500), so SUBTOTAL returns 900 while SUM on the same range still shows 2100.

tips: Keep the SUBTOTAL cell outside the filtered range, otherwise the filter can hide the formula itself.
Nested SUBTOTALs inside the range are ignored automatically, which stops per-group subtotal rows from being double counted.

sections.title: Code 9 vs Code 109: Manually Hidden Rows
sections.content: Codes 101 to 111 are the stricter twins of 1 to 11. They skip manually hidden rows in addition to filtered ones. Use 109 when rows are hidden by hand (Format > Hide Rows) and should stay out of the total; use 9 when a manual hide is just a temporary visual tidy-up that must not move the number.

example.explanation: No filter is applied but row 5 (amount 500) is manually hidden. Code 109 returns 2100 - 500 = 1600, whereas code 9 still returns the full 2100.

tips: The same pairing covers the other aggregates: 1/101 AVERAGE, 2/102 COUNT, 3/103 COUNTA, 4/104 MAX, 5/105 MIN.
Pick one convention for the workbook and write it on the sheet — mixing 9 and 109 produces two totals that differ by exactly the manually hidden rows.

sections.title: Count and Average the Rows You Can See
sections.content: Codes 2 and 3 are the counting pair: 2 behaves like COUNT and counts numeric cells only, 3 behaves like COUNTA and counts any non-empty cell. Both respect the filter, which makes them the quickest way to label a filtered report with a meaningful row count instead of a fixed one.

example.explanation: With Widget filtered, three of the six product cells remain visible, so SUBTOTAL(3, ...) returns 3. A plain COUNTA on the same range still returns 6.

tips: Use SUBTOTAL(2, range) when a column mixes text and numbers and only numeric entries should be counted.
SUBTOTAL(1, range) gives a filter-aware average; 101 additionally ignores manually hidden rows.

sections.title: Adding Criteria to a Sum of Visible Rows
sections.content: SUBTOTAL takes no criteria argument, and SUMIFS ignores visibility entirely. The workaround is to use SUBTOTAL(103, ...) as a visibility flag — 1 for a visible row, 0 for a hidden one — and multiply it by your condition inside SUMPRODUCT. AGGREGATE(9, 5, range) is the shorter Excel-only alternative, but it does not exist in Google Sheets, so the SUMPRODUCT pattern is the portable one.

example.explanation: Unfiltered, every row reports a visibility flag of 1, so the formula sums the Widget amounts (100 + 300 + 500) = 900. Filter the list to Widget + South and only row 4 stays visible, so the same formula returns 300.

tips: OFFSET is volatile and recalculates on every edit. On large tables build a helper column with =SUBTOTAL(103,$A2) and reference that instead.
In Excel 2010 or later, =AGGREGATE(9,5,$C$2:$C$7) is shorter and also ignores hidden rows — but Google Sheets has no AGGREGATE, so keep it out of shared sheets.

functionsUsed.name: SUM
functionsUsed.description: SUM adds all the numbers in a range of cells and returns the total.

functionsUsed.name: SUMIFS
functionsUsed.description: SUMIFS adds values that satisfy multiple criteria across one or more ranges.

functionsUsed.name: SUMPRODUCT
functionsUsed.description: SUMPRODUCT multiplies corresponding components of one or more arrays and returns the sum of those products. It is also widely used for conditional sums and counts without array-entry.

summary: Filter-aware totals come down to one function: SUBTOTAL(9, range) sums what you can see, 109 also drops manually hidden rows, and 2/3 count visible rows without a helper column. When criteria are needed as well, multiply a SUBTOTAL(103, ...) visibility flag into SUMPRODUCT — or use AGGREGATE(9,5,...) if the workbook never leaves Excel.
